source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Bartlett took the word schema from the neurologist Head (1920) and said he disliked it. He redefined it as an active organisation of past reactions or experiences, not a store of traces.
numbers: Head (1920) used schema for a postural model. Bartlett criticised three points: the cortex as storehouse, the phrase rising into consciousness, and the term itself being too definite and too sketchy.
quote: Schema refers to an active organisation of past reactions, or of past experiences
limits: He wrote that organised setting or active, developing patterns would be better terms. The word later hardened into a fixed-structure idea he did not intend.
agent_relevance: Our lesson store should hold active patterns that get rebuilt for the task, not frozen records.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Method of repeated reproduction: a subject studies a story, reproduces it from memory first after about 15 minutes, then again at longer and longer intervals. Bartlett used it to find the common types of change in normal remembering.
numbers: First reproduction usually after 15 minutes. Verbal and graphic material. He reports detail only for one story, The War of the Ghosts, out of many thousands of cases he says he collected.
limits: Instructions were informal and not standardised. Bartlett himself warned that frequent reproduction makes a form stereotyped fast, so results are a section of an incomplete process. No statistics are reported.
agent_relevance: Repeated retell-and-store loops (summarise, store, retrieve, summarise) are exactly this paradigm. Drift is expected, not a bug.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Why The War of the Ghosts: a Native American folk tale (from Boas) from a culture far from his Cambridge subjects. Events had no obvious link, and the ending was supernatural. This made it good material for forced transformation.
numbers: Original story about 330 words. Subjects were educated adults. The series in this chapter used twenty subjects (seven women, thirteen men).
limits: The story was adapted from a translation, so the stimulus was not the raw oral text. Small N, no control for rote learning.
agent_relevance: A deliberately foreign input is the stress test for any prior-driven memory. Test our agent on tasks that break its usual template.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Observed distortion types in repeated reproduction of the ghost story: omission of detail, rationalisation of the odd parts, loss of proper names and numbers, transformation of the title, and a prepotent theme that organises the rest.
numbers: Title omitted by 7 of 20 subjects and transformed by 10 of the others. Items that changed most: title, proper names, definite numbers, the meaning of the ghosts, canoes.
quote: Whenever anything appeared incomprehensible, or queer, it was either omitted or explained.
limits: Counts are given for a few features only. Rationalisation was often unwitting, which makes it hard to separate from simple guessing or from demand effects.
agent_relevance: Anything odd in a task statement may be dropped or smoothed by the model. Keep the raw statement on disk and re-check against it.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Subject N turned 'ghosts' into a clan name, which made the story make sense. He was satisfied with this, and a fortnight later the ghosts were even more prominent. The error grew with each recall, and confidence grew with it.
numbers: One subject, reproduced at first reading, then after a fortnight. N=1 case study.
quote: This subject was extremely well satisfied with his version
limits: Anecdotal. Satisfaction was not measured, only described by Bartlett.
agent_relevance: This is the fixation pattern. A wrong reframe that makes things coherent feels right and persists. Coherence is not evidence (supports G3).

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Affective determination: whether the excuses of the young man survived depended on the subject's own situation. Wartime men dropped the 'no arrows' excuse more often than the 'relatives' excuse.
numbers: Arrows excuse omitted by half of the 20 subjects. Of the 10 who kept it, 6 were women. Only 2 subjects omitted the reference to relatives, apart from long-delay reproductions.
limits: Bartlett calls it a possible case. Small groups, no tests, confounded sex and war exposure.
agent_relevance: What is kept is chosen by the current goal and mood. A solver with a goal will keep goal-matching lines of a lesson and lose the rest.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Bartlett's theory of remembering: the organism can turn round upon its own schemata and infer the probable constituents that must have occurred. Remembering is a constructive justification of an attitude toward a mass of past reactions.
numbers: Chapter on a theory of remembering, about pp. 197-214. Claims that a literal storehouse of traces is not what happens in most remembering.
quote: Remembering is a constructive justification of this attitude
limits: Brewer and Nakamura (1984) point out he wrote two versions: an official pure-reconstructive one and an unofficial one that keeps some specific traces.
agent_relevance: A memory call in our agent should be a rebuild from stored pieces plus the current task, and the rebuild should be checked against a stored trace.

source: Bartlett (1932) Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology (1995 Cambridge reprint)
finding: Literal recall is rare and unimportant in a changing world. Remembering is like a skilled stroke in a game: it is built afresh each time from the prior balance of postures and the needs of the moment.
numbers: Compares recall of an old story with constructing a new story from given outline material: subjects' attitudes were strikingly similar in both cases.
limits: Qualitative claim from informal experiments. The comparison of old story vs constructed story is not scored.
agent_relevance: Retrieval and generation are the same act for an LLM. Do not treat a recalled lesson as ground truth.

source: Minsky (1974) A Framework for Representing Knowledge, MIT AI Memo 306
finding: A frame is a data structure for a stereotyped situation, with fixed top levels and terminals (slots) that take specific values. Terminals come filled with default assignments that are attached loosely so new items can displace them. A failed match calls up a replacement frame from a retrieval network.
numbers: Frame-systems share terminals across viewpoints. No experiments; this is a design proposal with worked examples in vision, language and imagery.
quote: A frame is a data-structure for representing a stereotyped situation
limits: Minsky says frames are incomplete and can impose stereotypes on reality and jump to conclusions. He notes that old assumptions, once acquired, are persistent and hard to revise (his Boston example).
agent_relevance: Direct template for a schema: fixed goal, slots, defaults, match-failure trigger. Defaults are the place where fixation hides.

source: Minsky (1974) A Framework for Representing Knowledge, MIT AI Memo 306
finding: Minsky says the earliest frames tend to become the centres (capitals) of later ones, because each success adds another pointer to them. The structure of the previous structure dominates the later one.
numbers: Qualitative argument; no numbers.
quote: at each step the structure of the previous structure dominates the acquisition of the later
limits: A claim about development, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Early lessons in a store gain pull over time. Rank retrieved lessons by recent verified use, not by how often they were pointed at.

source: Anderson and Pichert (1977/1978) Recall of previously unrecallable information following a shift in perspective (Tech Report 41)
finding: Students read a story about two boys skipping school from either a burglar or a home-buyer view, then recalled it twice. After a shift of perspective, they recalled more of what was important to the new view that they had not recalled before.
numbers: Exp 1: N=39. Story 373 words, 72 idea units. Shifters recalled +7.1% of new-perspective information; the no-shift group recalled -2.9% of the same kind; F(1,35)=9.57, p<.01. Loss of old-perspective information: -7.2% vs no change, F(1,35)=2.22, p<.15 (n.s.). Exp 2: N=16, all shifted, no control: +10% new-view information (t(15)=3.02, p<.01), -21% old-view (t(15)=5.36, p<.01).
limits: College students, one story. Exp 2 had no control group. Interview reports: 7 of 12 described a schema retrieval plan and 6 said it jogged memory; self-report is weak. Output editing and guessing are not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Information is stored but not reachable without the right schema cue. A lesson store needs several retrieval views; one query frame hides the rest.

source: Anderson and Pichert (1977/1978) Recall of previously unrecallable information following a shift in perspective (Tech Report 41)
finding: The report lists ways a schema could raise recall of important text: attention at encoding, ideational scaffolding at encoding, retrieval plan, output editing, and inferential reconstruction. Their data support a retrieval role independent of encoding.
numbers: Cites Bransford and Johnson: a context given before a hard passage helps, given after does not. Cites Bartlett and others: importations rise with the length of the retention interval. Cites Newman 1939 and Bower 1976: important elements survive delay, unimportant ones drop.
limits: Importation growth with delay could also reflect inference at reading (Royer 1977). The report says the interpretations are open.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean list of functions a schema can serve; each needs a separate test in our agent (attend, store, retrieve, edit, infer).

source: Pichert and Anderson (1977) Taking different perspectives on a story (Tech Report 14)
finding: Importance of the same story elements depends on the reader's perspective, and recall follows the assigned perspective. Rated importance of idea units barely correlates across perspectives.
numbers: Exp 1: 63 raters; split-half reliability .91 to .98; Kendall tau across perspectives within a story about .11 (the florist-shipwrecked pair was higher). Exp 2: N=113 (56 House story, 57 Island story). Importance effect on immediate recall F(2,202)=103.4, omega-squared=.23. One-week delayed recall (45 and 47 students): importance F(2,160)=9.18, omega-squared=.03. Operative-perspective rating predicted recall better than non-operative ratings in 5 of 6 story-perspective cases. The homebuyer perspective failed to give the expected result in the regression.
limits: Undergraduates, two stories, one failing subcase (homebuyer). Effect size is medium at immediate test and small at delay.
agent_relevance: The same input produces different stored content under different frames. Set the frame deliberately, and log which frame was active when a lesson was written.

source: Brewer and Nakamura (1984) The nature and functions of schemas (Tech Report 325)
finding: Brewer and Nakamura split Bartlett into an official pure reconstructive theory and an unofficial partial reconstructive one. They argue the pure version has a fatal flaw: it allows no recall of unique episodic details, such as that the typewriter was an Underwood.
numbers: Five schema processes proposed: (a) direct attention, (b) framework to preserve episodic information, (c) combine generic with episodic information into an instantiated memory, (d) retrieval aid, (e) edit output.
quote: it has a fatal flaw--it allows no recall of unique episodic information
limits: Review of the 1970s-80s literature, using a subtractive logic on other authors' experiments; reanalysis, not new data.
agent_relevance: Our rebuild-at-recall design needs to keep raw traces beside the schema, otherwise exact details (numbers, names) are lost.

source: Brewer and Nakamura (1984) The nature and functions of schemas (Tech Report 325)
finding: Their summary of Brewer and Treyens (1981): people waited in an office and then did recall and recognition. They reported office-schema objects that were not present. In verbal recognition, a different group's schema-expectancy scores correlated highly with false recognition of absent items.
numbers: Reported as a high positive correlation; the report gives no coefficient. Original study not opened this session (no free full text found).
limits: Second-hand account. Exact N and rates need the primary paper (Cognitive Psychology 13:207-230).
agent_relevance: The false-memory risk is highest for items the schema predicts. Check predicted but unobserved items first.

source: Brewer and Nakamura (1984) The nature and functions of schemas (Tech Report 325)
finding: In Brewer and Treyens, schema-related objects that were strongly recognised were much more likely to be written down in recall than schema-unrelated ones. They argued the office schema acted as a retrieval device.
numbers: Qualitative summary only.
limits: Second-hand; part of a subtractive-logic reanalysis in which Brewer and Nakamura say several studies support mechanisms different from those the authors claimed.
agent_relevance: Schema as cue explains why schema-consistent items come out first. Use schema-inconsistent probes to test recall.

source: Brewer and Treyens (1981) Role of schemata in memory for places
finding: Participants waited briefly in a graduate student office that held many expected objects and a few odd ones, then were tested for recall, recognition and drawing. They recalled objects consistent with an office that were absent, books being the best known example.
numbers: Not verified by reading the paper. Wikipedia's schema page and the Brewer-Nakamura report agree on the false-books finding. N and exact rates not recorded here.
limits: Single room, one lab. Later work not checked in this pass.
agent_relevance: Treat as the textbook case of prior-filled gaps; get the exact table in another angle before relying on percentages.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11-01) Schema (psychology)
finding: Lineage: Bartlett (1932) after Head; Piaget (1952) as the first developmental theory of schemas; Anderson (1977) schema theory; Minsky frames, then scenes and scripts; Rumelhart's 1980s psychological theory of complex knowledge.
numbers: Describes Minsky's frame as fixed information plus slots that accept ranges of values with defaults when the world gives none.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, used only for lineage.
agent_relevance: Lineage check only.

source: Rumelhart and Norman (1978); Rumelhart (1980) Schemata: the building blocks of cognition
finding: Rumelhart treats schemata as data structures with variables, embedded in each other, that act like procedures to interpret input. Learning has three modes: accretion (add facts to existing schemas), tuning (adjust a schema to fit), restructuring (create a new schema).
numbers: Not opened this session; from the literature as cited.
limits: Not read. Details to confirm in another angle.
agent_relevance: Maps to our lesson store: accretion = add a lesson, tuning = amend, restructuring = rewrite the subgoal library. Restructuring is the rare costly one.

source: Alba and Hasher (1983) Is memory schematic?
finding: Psychological Bulletin review that tests five processes of schema theory: selection, abstraction, interpretation, integration, deterministic reconstruction. Argued the evidence for them is weaker than usually claimed, and that people retain much specific detail. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not opened. Do not quote numbers from this line.
limits: From memory of the paper's thesis; confirm elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Argues against building the agent as a pure schema machine; keep verbatim traces.

source: Bergman and Roediger (1999) Can Bartlett's repeated reproduction experiments be replicated?
finding: Memory and Cognition paper repeating Bartlett's paradigm with controlled instructions and more subjects. Cited as finding that omissions and some gist changes appear and grow with delay, but that the rich rationalisation Bartlett described was rarer and that instructions mattered. Not opened.
numbers: Exact numbers not recorded. Not opened.
limits: Reconstructed from citation memory; confirm elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Do not assume large distortion. Measure it on our own loop.

source: Gauld and Stephenson (1967) Some experiments relating to Bartlett's theory of remembering
finding: British Journal of Psychology paper cited as showing that telling subjects to be accurate reduced Bartlett-style errors a lot, which suggests that part of the distortion came from loose instructions. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Citation memory; confirm elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Accuracy instructions and a check step may cut invented content; test it.

source: Wynn and Logie (1998) The veracity of long-term memory: did Bartlett get it wrong?
finding: Memory paper that had students recall The War of the Ghosts repeatedly over months. Cited as finding recall that was fairly stable and not strongly distorted. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Citation memory; confirm elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Repeated recall may fix a version rather than drift it, which matches Bartlett's own note on fixed forms.

source: Roediger and McDermott (1995) Creating false memories: remembering words not presented in lists
finding: Word lists built around a missing critical word (sleep) produce high rates of false recall and recognition of that word. Not opened; rates not recorded.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Citation memory. The paradigm is associative, not schema based.
agent_relevance: Gist-consistent lures are the hardest errors for any associative memory, including an LLM's.

source: Huff, Bodner and Fawcett (2021) Manipulations of list type in the DRM paradigm: a review (Frontiers)
finding: Review of what drives DRM false memory: activation-monitoring (spreading activation), fuzzy-trace (verbatim vs gist traces) and global matching models such as MINERVA2. None of the three explains all results.
numbers: Text states that none of the theories readily account for all of the results when list type (associative vs categorical) is varied. It also cites Hintzman (1986) 'Schema abstraction in a multiple-trace memory model'.
limits: The DRM paradigm is word lists, not stories or scenes; links to schemas are by analogy.
agent_relevance: There are three rival mechanisms for the same false-memory effect. A scaffold against fabrication should not assume one mechanism.

source: Hintzman (1986) Schema abstraction in a multiple-trace memory model
finding: MINERVA 2 stores only separate episodic traces, with no stored schema, yet at retrieval it shows prototype and schema-abstraction effects. This is a competing explanation: schema behaviour without schema storage. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Citation memory, via the DRM review.
agent_relevance: A retrieval store that keeps raw episodes and computes the gist at query time may need no separate schema store.

source: Dasgupta, Lampinen et al (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models and humans both reason better when the content fits real-world belief, a schema-like prior. Models showed content effects on natural language inference, syllogisms and the Wason selection task.
numbers: Wason task: content advantage for realistic rules in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 (all z>2.2, p<0.03); PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 only marginal (z about 1.78, p about 0.08). Quoted prior human work: 90% of the time people called an invalid syllogism valid when the conclusion was believable.
limits: Abstract tasks, 2022-era models. Few-shot examples gave only mild gains. Not a memory test.
agent_relevance: A model's world-knowledge prior leaks into logic. Test with belief-conflicting and nonsense-content variants of our own tasks.

source: Kumar, Marjieh et al (2024) Comparing abstraction in humans and LLMs using multimodal serial reproduction
finding: Serial reproduction (Bartlett's method) with humans and GPT-4 on binary grid boards. Adding language to the chain makes human boards simpler and more compressible; GPT-4 changes much less.
numbers: 348 Prolific participants. Chain velocity higher in multimodal chains: humans t(198)=4.05, p<.0001; GPT-4 t(198)=-7.01, p<.0001. GPT-4 chain velocity above humans in both conditions (t(198)=6.97 and 10.87). Two-way ANOVA subject x modality interaction significant for all complexity measures.
limits: Grid boards, not stories. GPT-4 chains used 10 iterations.
agent_relevance: GPT-4 relies on language form by default. A text-only agent will compress and smooth through its own prior in every retell step.

source: Wang, Panaganti and Zhou (2026) More memory, worse agents: error reproduction and anti-persistence in LLM agents
finding: Stored abstractions (rules, summaries, skills) can spread errors: a wrong rule shapes the next trajectory, which is then used to write new rules that repeat the error. Keeping trajectories and rebuilding guidance on demand, then discarding it, does better.
numbers: ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld; backbones Llama-4-Scout, Qwen3-Coder-Next, Gemma-4-31B-it; 3 seeds; 10 memory updates. Anti-persistence beat trajectory and abstraction memory in all nine settings and joint memory in eight, with the lowest mean LLM-call cost. Abstraction and joint memory were below trajectory memory in seven of nine settings. Reflexion averaged 52.9%.
limits: Preprint (Oct 2026), not peer reviewed. Final per-setting means were not copied here.
agent_relevance: Strong direct match to Bartlett's reconstruction-versus-storage question and to schema fixation. Store raw traces, rebuild guidance per task, discard it.

source: Chen et al (2025) Schema for in-context learning (SA-ICL)
finding: A schema, here a short template of the key inferential steps extracted from one good example, added to the prompt, raises accuracy on hard science questions. The authors say models do not form or use such schemas well on their own.
numbers: GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro Stat and Finance; seven LLMs. Up to 36.19% improvement when the single demonstration is of high quality. Table rows seen: +4.9 and +6.4 points against +0.6 and +0.3 for plain one-shot in two settings, and +4.3 versus -0.8 in a third.
limits: Preprint; the 36.19% is a best case, defined by high example quality. Gains differ by dataset.
agent_relevance: Explicit schema scaffolds help when the demonstration is good. This is the positive side to weigh against the fixation risk.

source: van Kesteren, Rijpkema, Ruiter and Fernandez (2013) Consolidation differentially modulates schema effects on memory for items and associations (PLoS ONE)
finding: Boundary condition for the schema memory benefit. Schema-congruent visuo-tactile pairs were better remembered, but the effect for item recognition only appeared after consolidation, while for associations it was already present at once and shrank over time.
numbers: 76 Dutch female students, 3 delays (0, 20, 48 hours), 3x2 between design. Item recognition d-prime: delay x congruency F(2,66)=5.04. Associative memory: congruency main effect F(1,66)=17.59, p<.001, no interaction with delay.
limits: All female right-handed students, one stimulus set made in the lab.
agent_relevance: A schema benefit is not automatic. It depends on memory type and delay, so test it per retrieval mode.

source: Sweegers, Coleman, van Poppel, Cox and Talamini (2015) Mental schemas hamper memory storage of goal-irrelevant information
finding: When a schema was enough to do the task, schema-congruent items were stored worse: item memory and context memory were both impaired, with larger loss for context. The EEG recollection signal was smaller for congruent items.
numbers: Faces coupled with homes; parietal old/new ERP at 500-800 ms. The abstract reports substantial impairments in item memory and larger ones in context memory. Per-condition numbers not copied.
limits: Single lab; EEG sample size not recorded here.
agent_relevance: When the schema is enough, detail is not stored. If our agent follows the template it will not record the odd facts that later matter.

source: Frank, Montaldi, Wittmann and Talmi (2018) Beneficial and detrimental effects of schema incongruence on memory for contextual events (Learning and Memory)
finding: Incongruent components were remembered worse than congruent ones, despite more fixations at encoding. Incongruence helped in some cases against an unrelated baseline, for example reduced interference for the D-A pair.
numbers: Events of four overlapping pairs (A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A); recognition then cued recall; experiment 2 with eye tracking; one analysis had 31 participants (30 analysed). Recognition and recall reduced for incongruent versus congruent components across experiments.
limits: Effects depend on task demands. Mixed picture: schema-congruent benefit, incongruent surprise benefit against baseline, and the surprise did not integrate into the episode.
agent_relevance: Surprise gets attention but not integration. A check that fires on mismatch must also write the surprise into the structure, not only flag it.

source: Ghosh and Gilboa (2014) What is a memory schema? A historical perspective on current neuroscience literature (Neuropsychologia)
finding: Review proposing four features of a memory schema: an associative network structure, a basis in multiple episodes, lack of unit detail, and adaptability. Argues that much neuroscience work uses the word loosely. Not opened (paywalled).
numbers: Not opened. Crossref lists 455 citations.
limits: Four-feature list from citation memory; confirm elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Gives a test for whether our stored object counts as a schema: built from many episodes, drops unit detail, can adapt.

source: Tse et al (2007) Schemas and memory consolidation (Science)
finding: Rats with a learned schema of flavour-place pairs learned new pairs in one trial and consolidated them faster, becoming independent of the hippocampus within about 48 hours. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened. Europe PMC lists about 918 citations.
limits: From citation memory, details unchecked.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that fit with a prior structure speeds consolidation: add a lesson fast when it fits the library, slowly when it does not.
